Volcano. A geological opening in Earth's crust through which molten rock, ash, gases, and rock fragments erupt onto the surface. Volcanoes are windows into Earth's interior and drivers of planetary geology and climate, ranging from quietly flowing shield volcanoes to catastrophically explosive stratovolcanoes, and their distribution marks the boundaries of tectonic plates and regions of crustal instability.

Volcanoes form at three main tectonic settings: divergent plate boundaries where mid-ocean ridges spread apart, convergent boundaries at subduction zones, and hotspots where magma rises within the planet's interior. When lava cools rapidly at the surface, it forms extrusive igneous rocks like basalt, andesite, and rhyolite. Shield volcanoes like those in Hawaii erupt fluid lava and build broad, gentle slopes, while stratovolcanoes like Mount Fuji and Mount Vesuvius explode violently and form steep cones.

When volcanoes erupt, they inject ash and sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere, temporarily cooling the planet by reflecting sunlight. Mount Vesuvius erupted in seventy-nine AD and Mount Krakatoa in eighteen eighty-three, both events that reshaped human civilization through destruction and left permanent marks on cultural memory. Volcanoes are not limited to Earth either. Jupiter's moon Io and Saturn's moon Enceladus exhibit cryovolcanism, eruptions of water ice and organic compounds instead of silicate magma.

The ground around volcanoes is extraordinarily fertile. Regions like Italy and the base of Mount Fuji support dense populations despite the eruption risk. The lava's composition, especially its silica content, determines how the volcano will behave. Low-silica basalt flows gently from the vent, while high-silica rhyolite traps gases inside and explodes catastrophically.

Volcanic hazards are diverse and severe. Lava flows consume everything in their path, while ash clouds can travel and block out the sun. Lahars are mudflows of volcanic debris that can sweep away communities. Pyroclastic flows—clouds of hot gas and rock—race down mountainsides at tremendous speeds. Toxic gas emissions can travel miles downwind. Dormancy does not guarantee safety. Many volcanoes labeled extinct have reawakened after centuries or even millennia of silence.

Magma is the molten rock that powers volcanic eruptions. Igneous rock forms from volcanic activity and defines the extrusive category of rocks. Plate tectonics provides the tectonic framework explaining where and why volcanoes occur. Mineral composition and crystallization at high temperatures shape volcanic rocks. Cryovolcanism extends volcanic phenomena beyond rocky planets to the icy bodies of the outer solar system.
